say.text: Start with a correct plan. A 35-year-old man has a primary, reducible, unilateral groin lump, and his surgeon is trained in open repair.

Step 1: the lump is clinically evident, so no imaging. Step 2: **Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair**, the standard open repair for an adult. Step 3: warn him about ilioinguinal nerve injury, the nerve most at risk in open repair.
Now a peer's plan for a 6-month-old boy with a reducible right groin swelling that appears on crying. One step is wrong.
1. Examine: reducible, clinically evident. 2. Herniotomy: high ligation and excision of the sac. 3. Lichtenstein mesh placed over the posterior wall. 4. Discharge the same day.
Which step is wrong?

choices.label: Step 1: no imaging; the lump is clinically evident
Step 2: herniotomy, high ligation and excision of the sac
Step 3: Lichtenstein mesh placed over the posterior wall
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what a child's groin defect actually is before you judge each step.
Tempting: a groin lump you cannot see into makes a scan feel careful.
But a clinically evident hernia is a clinical diagnosis. Step 1 is right, and imaging would not change the plan.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check this one: imaging is for an occult or complicated hernia, not for a visible lump.

say.text: Tempting: if you think every hernia needs its back wall fixed, herniotomy alone looks incomplete.
It is not incomplete. In a child herniotomy alone is the operation of choice, because the defect is a patent processus vaginalis and the posterior wall is normal.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look again: in a child the open sac is the problem, and excising it is the whole repair.

say.text: Step 3 is the error. Mesh reinforcement answers an adult's weak posterior wall.
A child's hernia is a patent processus vaginalis with a normal wall, so herniotomy alone is the repair. Steps 1 and 2 are right.
Good. Now the reason. Why does step 3 not belong in this child's repair?

choices.label: A child's posterior wall is normal; nothing is weak to mesh
Mesh would restrict growth of the child's abdominal wall
Children's tissues are too fragile to hold any mesh or sutures
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask where the hole is in a child: in the back wall, or in the sac?
Tempting: mesh feels like the safe reinforcement whatever the age.
Mesh does not restrict growth, and the wall is not the weak point here. The problem is the open sac, which herniotomy closes.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the age qualifier: mesh is an adult's answer to a weak wall.

say.text: Tempting: a child's tissues do feel delicate in the theatre.
Tissue fragility is not the reason. A child's wall is normal, and herniotomy needs no mesh or extra suture line.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the sac from the wall: a child's trouble is the sac.

say.text: The reason: the defect is a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall, so there is nothing to reinforce.
Herniotomy alone is the operation of choice for a child.
Next, a peer's plan for a 50-year-old man with a primary, reducible, unilateral hernia. His surgeon is trained in open repair. One step is wrong.
1. Examine: clinically evident, no imaging. 2. Bassini repair, the classic open repair. 3. Warn about ilioinguinal nerve injury. 4. Discharge the next day.
Which step is wrong?

choices.label: Step 2: Bassini repair, the classic open repair
Step 3: warn about ilioinguinal nerve injury
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which repair current practice uses for a primary adult hernia, and what the older key expected.
Tempting: thigh numbness after groin surgery makes the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve feel like the risk, so a warning about the other nerve looks misdirected.
But open repair puts the ilioinguinal nerve at risk; the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is the laparoscopic risk. Step 3 is correct.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie the nerve to the approach: the field of dissection decides which nerve is at risk.

say.text: Step 2 is the error. Bassini is the older key; current practice favours tension-free mesh.
Step 3 is right: in open repair the ilioinguinal nerve is the one most at risk, giving numbness at the root of the penis and upper medial thigh.
Which fact explains why Bassini is not today's standard open repair?

choices.label: It sutures the conjoint tendon to the inguinal ligament under tension
It is the standard open repair; mesh is an optional add-on
It is a mesh repair, so it counts as a hernioplasty
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask how the two sides of the canal are brought together in this repair.
Tempting: Bassini is the name every textbook gives the classic open repair.
It was the standard once, and older keys expected it. Current practice has moved to mesh, so Bassini is not the standard now.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the date: Bassini is the older key, not today's standard.

say.text: Tempting: Bassini closes the hernia with sutures that look like a modern closure, so it can seem like a mesh hernioplasty.
Bassini uses the patient's own tissue, so it is a herniorrhaphy. A mesh is what makes a repair a hernioplasty.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so sort the terms by what is added to the sac excision: tissue or mesh.

say.text: The reason: Bassini sutures the conjoint tendon to the inguinal ligament under tension, a tissue repair, so it is not today's standard.
A tense, tender, irreducible groin swelling, with vomiting and a toxic patient. Nothing is reducing it.
What do you do first?

choices.label: Resuscitate and take to emergency surgery
Attempt gentle then firm manual reduction
Request an ultrasound of the groin
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask first whether the bowel can still be alive, and what that decides before any reduction.
Tempting: reducing first is the habit for any reducible hernia, and it looks quick.
But when strangulation is suspected, forceful taxis is avoided: it can push gangrenous bowel back or cause reduction en masse.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check viability before any reduction: a strangulated hernia needs emergency surgery.

say.text: Tempting: a scan feels careful, and ultrasound is the test you would order for an occult hernia.
This patient is toxic with an irreducible, tender lump, so surgery now comes first; a scan would only delay the bowel rescue.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two cases: imaging answers an uncertain lump, not a strangulated one.

say.text: Resuscitate and go to emergency surgery. The first question is whether bowel is viable, and that comes before any reduction.
A 58-year-old man has a primary, unilateral, reducible hernia. He is unfit for general anaesthesia, and his surgeon is trained in open repair.
Which repair fits him best?

choices.label: Bassini repair, the classic open repair
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which of his conditions rules out a general anaesthetic, and which repair that leaves.
Tempting: laparoscopic is the modern default, and newer seems better.
But laparoscopic repair needs general anaesthesia, and it is preferred for bilateral or recurrent hernias, not for every patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the qualifier: a general anaesthetic he cannot take rules the laparoscopic route out.

say.text: Tempting: Bassini is the classic name, so it feels like the safe open answer.
Older keys expected Bassini, but current practice for an adult open repair is Lichtenstein mesh. Bassini is not today's standard.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pair the old key with the new one: Bassini was expected, Lichtenstein is the standard.

say.text: Open Lichtenstein is the answer. Laparoscopic repair needs a general anaesthetic he cannot take, and open Lichtenstein is the adult standard.
After a TAPP repair, a man has chronic groin pain and thigh numbness. The tack was placed lateral to the gonadal vessels, below the iliopubic tract.
Which triangle did the tack enter?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask whether this tack would catch vessels or nerves, and which triangle holds which.
Tempting: both triangles are no-tack zones, so the doom triangle feels like the right one.
The doom triangle holds the external iliac vessels. This tack sat on the nerve side, in the triangle of pain, which holds the nerves.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so split the pair: vessels belong to doom, nerves to pain.

say.text: The triangle of pain. The gonadal vessels divide the two triangles, and this tack lay on the nerve side.
The triangle of doom holds the external iliac vessels, so separate vessel from nerve.
A surgeon excises the sac and darns the posterior wall with the patient's own tissue. No mesh is used.
What is this operation called?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what is added to the sac excision: nothing, the patient's own tissue, or a mesh?
Tempting: any posterior-wall repair sounds like reinforcement, and hernioplasty is the reinforcement term.
Hernioplasty means reinforcement with a prosthetic mesh. Here no mesh is used, so the term is herniorrhaphy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what is added: no mesh here means not hernioplasty.

say.text: Tempting: herniotomy is the sac step every repair starts with, so it can seem to name the whole operation.
Herniotomy is excision of the sac alone. Adding the posterior-wall repair with the patient's own tissue makes it herniorrhaphy.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so order the terms by what is added to the sac excision: nothing, own tissue, or mesh.

say.text: Herniorrhaphy: sac excision plus repair of the posterior wall with the patient's own tissue.
Herniotomy is sac excision alone; hernioplasty adds a prosthetic mesh.
